text: Discovery doesn't just scan in the abstract — Lesson 14 described what it does, but not yet what actually controls it. Two specific record types do that. A Discovery Schedule decides when Discovery runs and what IP range or network segment it scans. A probe decides what detail gets collected once a device is found. This lesson covers both, and the real order they work in together.

A Discovery Schedule defines timing — nightly, weekly, on demand — and scope, the specific IP range or network segment being scanned on that schedule. A probe is much narrower: a specific operation that collects one particular kind of information, like identifying an operating system, inventorying installed software, or reading CPU and memory specs. One instance typically has several schedules at once, each pointed at a different range, often because different segments need different scan frequencies or different MID Servers to reach them at all.

Discovery doesn't try to learn everything about every address in one pass. First, an initial scan — effectively a ping sweep or port scan — checks which addresses in the range have something listening at all. Second, for each one that responds, Discovery classifies what kind of device it actually is: a Windows server, a Linux server, a network switch, something else entirely. Third, only once it knows the device type does it run the specific set of probes appropriate to that type of device.

That phasing is deliberate, not incidental. Running every possible probe against every address would be slow, wasteful, and in many cases meaningless — asking a network switch to report its installed Windows software doesn't make sense, because the question simply doesn't apply to that device. Classifying first means Discovery only asks the questions that are relevant to what it actually found, which produces faster, cleaner, more accurate CMDB data than a one-size-fits-all scan of every address ever could.

Schedules control when Discovery runs and where it scans; probes control what gets collected, in a strict scan-then-classify-then-probe order, never all at once. Next: the difference between scanning broadly across many kinds of infrastructure and going deep on the dependency chain of one specific service.
